name: Todd Monken

views.text: A head coach is paid to deliver a winning team, and he has to prove it again every single day.
A quarterback competition is won over weeks of film, not one good or bad practice.
Let a quarterback play to his own strengths instead of making him into someone else.
You cannot control a game if you cannot run the ball, and abandoning the plan is on the play-caller.
After a loss, review the scheme, the coaching, the execution and the plan, and own your part first.
Good ideas come from anywhere, including a clip a player found online.
Pre-snap penalties end the drill; sloppy operation does not get extra reps.
If the defense is already good, do not change the scheme just to put your stamp on it.

signatures: takes the blame for an offensive failure before anyone else is mentioned
jokes about his age while saying he is a better coach now than ever
cuts a practice period short when the same mistake repeats
want: to prove a lifelong offensive journeyman can turn Cleveland into a winner as a first-time NFL head coach
fear: that an unsettled quarterback room sinks his first season before his offense gets a fair chance
voice: Blunt, passionate and self-deprecating; he speaks with emotion about earning the job every day and takes responsibility quickly when the offense fails. He is candid but careful on the quarterback race, refusing to crown anyone off one practice, and talks in detailed, practical football terms. Loud and demanding on the field.

evidence.summary: Hiring release: about 35 years coaching, Georgia coordinator for two straight national titles, earlier coordinator for Tampa Bay and Cleveland, Southern Miss head coach. Harbaugh describes a wide search and praises his leadership and system-building. Facts and a club statement.

At his introduction he calls Jackson underrated as a passer, especially deep, says his reputation was shaped by early doubts, sees the league moving toward mobile quarterbacks, and says he trusts DeCosta and Harbaugh. His own words before meeting Jackson.

evidence.publisher: Pro Football Talk (NBC Sports), Charean Williams
evidence.summary: Jackson says he sends Monken plays he spots and Monken practices them, calls his meeting rooms full of ideas and is glad he listens. Jackson's view in a preseason broadcast.

Feature (page undated; contents place it at the start of the 2023 season): funny, self-deprecating and relaxed off the field, intense and loud at practice; from a coaching family; aggressive but calculated, borrows ideas widely, gives candid feedback; says he learned from Cleveland and that Harbaugh's relationship skills let him coach less abrasively. Jackson calls him fun and empowering. Team site.

He takes responsibility for the AFC Championship loss, says execution problems start with him, admits the team had to run better and stick to its plan, and wants a faster, more consistent second season. His words.

evidence.publisher: Sports Illustrated (Ravens on SI), Josh Reed
evidence.summary: After Harbaugh publicly critiques his play-calling in a loss, he says nothing was new because they had already talked, describes reviewing scheme, coaching, execution and plan each week, owns the shortcomings and commits to more runs. His words, filtered by a fan-network writer.

AP report on his introduction in Berea: an emotionally charged opening about being paid to deliver a winning team and having to prove it daily; joking that at nearly 60 he is a far better coach than 15 to 20 years ago; keeping the defensive scheme regardless of coordinator; an open quarterback room including Sanders and Watson. GM Berry praises his adaptability in Baltimore. Shows public tone, not private manner.

Team-site report on the new OC's introduction: Switzer, who worked under Monken in Baltimore for three seasons, describes Monken as collaborative, a listener who takes input and makes decisions with the staff. A subordinate's favorable description.

Camp notes, July 29 to August 20: he gives no timeline on the starting quarterback, says it is too early to call a leader and avoids overreacting to single practices, alternates first-team reps and adjusts when the count tilts, stops a two-minute drill after repeated pre-snap penalties, wants the quarterback to play to his own strengths, and says the team belonged in joint practices. Daily beat notes.
